title: Nandi and Nahusha
hook: a boy becomes Shiva's own and a king of heaven becomes a snake, and Patanjali explains both
carry: as you act, so you become
tomorrow: the most generous king, in a well

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vrika's boon, won by fierce tapas and turned on its giver. Power isn't holiness; character is.

The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras names two stories together. The first is Nahusha, a good human king, made king of heaven while Indra is in hiding. The throne goes to his head. He makes the great sages carry his litter like servants, and when the sage Agastya is too slow, Nahusha strikes him with his foot. Agastya says: fall, and be a snake. And the king of heaven drops to earth as a python. The second is Nandi, a human boy who loved Shiva so wholly that he became Shiva's own.
screen: `A KING OF HEAVEN KICKS A SAGE.` → `FALL, AND BE A SNAKE.` → `A BOY BECOMES SHIVA'S OWN.`

segments.voice: One went down, one went up, and Patanjali says it's the same law. Sutra 4.2: the change into another kind of being comes from nature overflowing. Sutra 4.3: your deeds don't set nature moving; they only pierce the barrier, like a farmer. The commentary pictures him at a full canal. He doesn't carry the water to his field in buckets. He cuts the little earth wall, and the water runs in by itself. Nature is already full. Your actions decide which wall gets cut. Nandi's devotion cut one. Nahusha's pride cut another. Here's the Hindu teaching, in the Upanishad's own plain words: as you act, as you live, so you become. Do good, become good; do harm, become harmful. That's karma, and the same Upanishad carries it into rebirth: what you're becoming doesn't stop at one body. Nahusha's story doesn't end in the dirt. Ages later, in the forest, the python seizes Bhima, and Yudhishthira answers its questions about who is truly a brahmin. Not birth, he says, but truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct, kindness. When the questions are answered, Nahusha is freed. Another wall cut. And Nandi is still at his post. In Shiva temples his image sits facing the shrine, and in many of them devotees stop at Nandi and whisper their prayers in his ear, because he's the one who never takes his eyes off Shiva. That's the farmer's lesson at both ends. You don't make the water. You choose the channel, and you turn into what you keep doing.
screen: `4.2: NATURE OVERFLOWING.` · `4.3: DEEDS CUT THE WALL.` · `DO GOOD, BECOME GOOD.` · `NAHUSHA, FREED BY ANSWERS.` · then, large: `AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Picture Nandi before the shrine, facing Shiva, steady. If you pray, sit the same way toward the form of God you love, and quietly tell one prayer, the way people whisper to Nandi. If you don't, choose one quality you want to grow into, and face it. When the mind wanders, turn back and face it again, like the bull who never looks away.
Kshetrika, the farmer, from kshetra, a field. Patanjali's picture for how deeds work: they don't make the water, they cut the wall, and nature flows into what you're becoming.
Your line: as you act, so you become. Nandi faced Shiva and became his. Day four hundred eighty-one, done.

Nandi.meaning: Shiva's devoted attendant, shown as the bull facing his shrine

Nahusha.meaning: a human king who ruled heaven, grew proud and fell as a python

Agastya.meaning: a great sage of the epics and Puranas

Yudhishthira.meaning: the eldest Pandava brother, known for dharma

Prakriti.meaning: nature: the stuff the mind and the world are made of

Kshetrika.meaning: a farmer, from kshetra, a field

sutra.meaning: a short, packed line of teaching; literally a thread
